nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: What initiative will be introduced to encourage the next generation of taxonomists?
nodes.answer: Awards for the best student papers on taxonomy and the best taxonomic treatments published in the journal will be introduced.
nodes.paragraph: I aim to streamline the publication pro- cess for taxonomists, ensuring their discoveries are shared with the world swiftly and efficiently. We will also actively seek out and promote special issues on relevant topics, including the pressing issue of global biodiversity conservation. The recent "30 30" target from the Global Biodiversity Framework underscores the urgency of this challenge, and we anticipate Kew Bulletin playing a vital role in disseminating research that contributes to its achievement. To nurture and encourage the next generation of taxonomists, we will introduce awards for the best student papers on taxonomy and the best taxonomic treatments published in the journal. These awards will recognise and celebrate outstanding contributions to the field, inspiring future generations of scientists. I am particularly passionate about supporting research that utilises natural history collections, espe- cially herbarium specimens. These collections are invaluable repositories of biodiversity data, yet their significance is often overlooked. I believe it is crucial to emphasise the importance of these collections and encourage researchers to fully leverage the data they contain, especially now that major herbaria worldwide, including Kew, have digitised most of their specimens, making digital images and associated data readily available to the global scientific community for biodi- versity research.

nodes.label: Taxonomy
nodes.question: How does the author want to involve taxonomists in the future of Kew Bulletin?
nodes.answer: The author invites passionate taxonomists interested in shaping the future of Kew Bulletin to contact them, indicating a desire to expand the reach and expertise of the editorial board.
nodes.paragraph: Of course, times are changing, and we must embrace the exciting new possibilities and challenges that lie ahead. One area of particular interest to me is the role of generative Al in scientific publishing. I believe these tools have the potential to revolution- ise how we write, review, and disseminate research. However, it is crucial to navigate this new landscape responsibly. We must ensure that Al is used ethically and transparently, and we must support authors in overcoming challenges and harnessing the power of these technologies. I believe that scientific research should be shared with a broad audience. Therefore, I will strive to enhance the journal S online presence through regu- lar social media posts to communicate the excitement and importance of plant and fungal taxonomy to the wider world. I am also committed to fostering a wel- coming and inclusive environment for all authors, reviewers, and readers. Kew Bulletin should be a space where diverse voices and perspectives are valued and celebrated. Finally, I want to expand the reach and expertise of the editorial board. If you are a passionate taxono- mist with a keen interest in shaping the future of Kew Bulletin, I encourage you to contact me.

nodes.question: Who can benefit from biodiversity information related to agricultural land use?
nodes.answer: Government agencies, research institutions, non-governmental organizations, businesses, and consumers can all benefit from biodiversity information related to agricultural land use.
nodes.paragraph: In these contexts, indicators are used to assess (bio-diversity) impacts linked to different LU change drivers, whichincludes accountability for historical impacts or identi cation of cur- rent pressures 4 6. Such biodiversity information is relevant not only to decisions on agricultural LU locally, but also those concerning supply-chain decisions downstream 7,8. Whether used by government agencies, research institutions, non-governmental organisations, businesses or consumers, relatingReceived: 6 May 2024 Accepted: 10 February 2025 Check for updates 1Senckenberg Biodiversity and Climate Research Centre, Frankfurt am Main, Germany.2Faculty of Biological Sciences, Goethe University Frankfurt, Frankfurt am Main, Germany.3Department of Space, Earth and Environment, Chalmers University of Technology, Gothenburg, Sweden.4Stockholm Environment Institute York, University of York, York, UK. e-mail: gabi.rabeschini@gmail.com ;martin.persson@chalmers.se Nature Communications I (2025) 16:1799 11234567890():, 1234567890():, biodiversity indicators to the agricultural LU drivers will be useful if it equips actors with robust information to address trade-offs betweenproduction, consumption and conservation. Policy makers may wishfor an indicator that is easy to implement and communicate; busi- nesses, for an easy-to-track, target oriented indicator; researchers, for an indicator that captures accurately as many aspects of biodiversity aspossible.

nodes.label: Taxonomy
nodes.question: Which sources were used for analyzing historical data of G. barbata?
nodes.answer: Historical data were collected from published articles, unpublished reports, and herbarium vouchers.
nodes.paragraph: The present study aims to (i) establish the current distribution of G. barbata along the French Mediterranean coasts including Corsica; (ii) reconstruct the past distribution using historical data; (iii) analyze the long-term evolution of the distribution to assess the status of the taxon and identify any potential causes of decline; and (iv) finally identify the potential benefits of implementing ecological restoration. Materials and methods Study area The Mediterranean coasts of France was considered in its entirety, from Cerb re (at the Spanish border) to Menton (at the Italian border), including Corsica. The area was divided into five administrative regions: French Catalonia and Languedoc, Western Provence, Eastern Provence, French Riviera, and Corsica (Fig. 1). Data collection Historical data Historical records of Gongolaria barbata were analysed from a variety of sources, including published articles, unpublished reports and herbarium vouchers. The majority of the printed documents are kept in the MACROPHYTES research platform of the Mediterranean Institute of Oceanography (MIO, Aix-Marseille University). Vouchers held in herbaria represent an invaluable source of data allowing the verification of specimen identification.
